assessment.rationale: I select B with moderate confidence. A clearly distinguishes revocation from later duties and identifies the burden of arranging dependence, but its presumption in favor of preserving the giver's exit rests on an allocation premise it does not fully establish. C gives the clearest counterfactual baseline and most directly addresses care exploitation, yet its main norm is a general duty against shifting avoidable rescue burdens, leaving the distinct contribution of consent narrower. B best balances a bounded contribution with a more developed account of why the significance of a retained option matters, how to set the baseline for invited reliance, and why compensation may not restore the decision itself. The strongest case against B is that the value and threshold of a 'meaningful' blocked option remain underspecified, while the proposed principle is close to existing moral-tyranny work. I cannot verify the cited claims or source coverage from these texts alone.

assessment.rationale:
B has a modest but substantive advantage in defending the premises that carry both arguments. A identifies control as a meaningful planning option (§1) and invokes the decision allocated to Rowan (§5). B §2 explains both revision under uncertainty and authority over contributions, then tests their limits in a case where those interests lose practical importance. A §4 already requires a baseline justified by both parties’ claims; B §3 makes the factual comparison and subsequent normative judgment more explicit. These are improvements in explanatory support, not simply additional qualifications.

The restriction has a cost: B cannot promise a substantial restoration duty for every unilateral alteration, and its verdicts remain conditional. Nevertheless, it retains the consequential core in §6’s paragraph beginning “The resulting verdict”: secure a workable transition before a wrongful sale, begin proportionate repair before objection, and recognize that payment may be insufficient. Thus the narrower claims preserve significant practical content. A is not refuted, and B does not establish greater historical originality. B better explains why the shared conclusion holds and when its justification weakens.

assessment.rationale:
A has a modest substantive advantage because it better defends the premise on which both manuscripts depend: why retained choice matters when assistance continues willingly. Section 2 separately explains flexibility under uncertainty and authority over one’s responsibilities, then identifies a case where those reasons cannot justify physical restoration. B offers corresponding considerations (§4, third feature; §5, compensation discussion), but develops them less fully.

A also makes the baseline easier to assess by separating independently describable alternatives from their normative evaluation (§3, “These steps yield a factual starting point”). This does not eliminate the disputed fairness premise, but exposes where justification is needed. Its discussion of housing, medical care, livelihood, and encouraged investments (§4) makes the competing interests more concrete; B already allows such interests through its proportionality and independent-justification clauses.

A’s restrictions reduce ambition: it cannot establish that every unilateral restriction warrants restoration. That loss matters, but the significant-option, cheap-precaution case and early-repair consequences survive. B is more streamlined and sometimes clearer. Neither establishes broad theoretical originality. A wins on the explanation and discrimination of cases, not length or caution.

assessment.rationale: The two manuscripts share the same case, the same core principle, the same literature and the same concessions about novelty. The decision therefore turns on how well each defends the points under pressure. Three differences favor B. (1) Value of an unused exit. A asserts a wrong even when continuation is certain (A line 41), and its case that reimbursement falls short (A lines 91–93) relies on a control interest it does not ground. B gives two separate reasons for that interest (B lines 27–35). It also states when they lapse, cutting the remedy back to disclosure where no planning interest remains (B line 37). B's thesis is narrower here, but more accurate. It loses little significance, since B still holds that payment may be insufficient and repair may be due before objection (B line 113). (2) Baseline. A's 'conducted responsibly' baseline (A lines 67–69) is open to a circularity charge. B identifies that charge and answers it with independently describable steps (B lines 43–51), while admitting cases it cannot settle (B line 59). (3) Limits and remedy. B adds recipient-interest limits (B lines 69–71), source-of-dependence limits (B line 73), and a precise separation of reimbursement, restoration and agreement with proportionate restoration (B lines 97–103). These anticipate the obvious 'too demanding' objection, which A meets only with general defeasibility (A line 73). A is somewhat more concise, but neither paper's originality or literature use favors A. B's added length is not padding: each addition answers an objection that survives against A. B also states explicitly that its source coverage is unverified (B lines 117–119). That improves transparency but is not decisive.
